# The Capability Horizon and Its Measurement {#sec-capability-horizon}

The frontier is no longer a leaderboard number. It is a moving horizon: a set
of task, reliability, cost, and oversight limits that move at different speeds.
Locating the frontier is therefore a measurement problem. A headline number is
useful only when its measurement contract travels with it: the system tested,
the tasks sampled, the resources allowed, the success threshold, and the
snapshot date.

The same evidence can support very different conclusions. A task horizon,
defined in the next section, is the length of task, counted in human working
time, that an agent completes at a given success rate. Rising horizons may
reflect durable progress, or part of the apparent acceleration may be a
compute-bought artifact, a gain that comes from larger compute budgets and would
not persist at a fixed budget. A model may beat an expert deliverable in a blind
comparison while failing to automate the surrounding job. A benchmark may rise
quickly because capability improved, because tools changed, or because the
instrument became easier to exploit. This chapter separates those claims instead
of compressing them into one score.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-horizon-contract
//| fig-cap: "A capability result is conditional on a measurement contract. Changing the system, task sample, resources, success threshold, or date creates a different result, even when the benchmark keeps the same name."
digraph {
  bgcolor="transparent";
  rankdir=TB;
  nodesep=0.2; ranksep=0.25;
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9, color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280", fillcolor="#f1ece1", penwidth=1.1];
  edge [color="#6b7280"];

  contract [label="system + scaffold\ntask sample\nresource budget\nsuccess rule + date"];
  claim [label="capability claim", color="#3b82f6", fontcolor="#3b82f6", penwidth=1.4];

  contract -> claim;
}
```

## A horizon is a fitted threshold

The task-completion horizon uses human completion time as a proxy for task
difficulty, then estimates how an agent's success rate changes as tasks become
longer. The duration it reports is the time a human needs, not the time the
agent runs. METR's original study focused mainly on self-contained software,
machine-learning, and cybersecurity tasks. Its result therefore describes a
fixed system and protocol on that task distribution, not the probability of
succeeding on every real-world task of the same duration [@kwa2025longtasks].

Let task $i$ have a positive human completion time $d_i$, where $i$ identifies
the task. For repeated attempt $r$, let $Y_{ir}=1$ when the evaluated system
succeeds and $Y_{ir}=0$ otherwise.
A simple version of the fitted model is

$$
\Pr(Y=1\mid d)=\sigma(\alpha-\beta\ln d),
\qquad
\sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}},
\qquad \beta>0.
$$

Here $Y$ is the binary outcome, $d$ is human completion time, $\alpha$ is the
fitted intercept, $\beta$ is the fitted slope, $\ln$ is the natural logarithm,
and $\sigma$ maps the fitted value to a probability. For a chosen success
threshold $q$, the corresponding horizon is

$$
h_q=\exp\!\left(\frac{\alpha-\operatorname{logit}(q)}{\beta}\right),
\qquad
\operatorname{logit}(q)=\ln\!\left(\frac{q}{1-q}\right).
$$

$h_q$ means the human-time duration at which the fitted success probability
equals $q$. It is an estimate with uncertainty, not an observed task boundary.
The model checkpoint, agent scaffold (the execution loop and prompts wrapped
around the model), tool access, task distribution, human-time baseline, repeated
attempts, token budget, time budget, scoring rule, and measurement date all
belong to its protocol.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-horizon-thresholds
//| fig-cap: "The same fitted success curve yields different horizons at different reliability thresholds. Their ratio is controlled by the fitted slope, so the 50%-to-80% gap is not a universal multiplier."
digraph {
  bgcolor="transparent";
  rankdir=TB;
  nodesep=0.2; ranksep=0.25;
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9, color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280", fillcolor="#f1ece1", penwidth=1.1];
  edge [color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280", fontsize=8];

  runs [label="repeated outcomes\nby human task time"];
  fit [label="fit success curve"];
  h50 [label="read h50 at 50%"];
  h80 [label="read h80 at 80%"];

  runs -> fit;
  fit -> h50 [label="threshold"];
  fit -> h80 [label="threshold"];
}
```

## The threshold changes the answer

The 50 percent horizon is easy to communicate, but many deployments need much
greater reliability. The 80 percent horizon comes from the same fitted curve.
Its distance from the 50 percent horizon is

$$
\frac{h_{0.5}}{h_{0.8}}
=\exp\!\left(\frac{\operatorname{logit}(0.8)}{\beta}\right).
$$

In words, the ratio depends on $\beta$, the fitted slope, so it is not a
universal constant. The original study found ratios around four to six for its
fits, while later model estimates varied more widely [@kwa2025longtasks]. A
statement such as “five times shorter” therefore describes one empirical fit and
does not carry over to other fits.

The following calculation uses 18 hours and 3.5 hours only as illustrative
midpoints of early-2026 reported ranges. It recovers the slope implied by those
two thresholds; it does not refit METR's task-level data.

:::: {.runnable}
```python
from math import log

h50 = 18.0
h80 = 3.5
beta = log(4.0) / log(h50 / h80)

print(f"fitted slope: {beta:.3f}")
print(f"50% / 80% horizon ratio: {h50 / h80:.3f}")
```
::::

A second intuition, kept separate from the fitted curve, explains why long
workflows can be fragile. If a task had $n$ independent, homogeneous steps, each
succeeding with probability $p$, its all-step success probability would be
$p^n$. Real agent trajectories do not satisfy that toy model's independence or
homogeneous steps assumptions, and the horizon studies do not identify step
failures as the mechanism, so the toy model is an illustration and not a causal
explanation. The recovery and error-compounding problems in @sec-machine-breaks
are related operational concerns; the horizon curve is not derived from them.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Constraint arrow

The threshold chosen at the measurement layer limits which tasks the autonomy
layer can safely take on. A 50 percent horizon is suitable for tracking
capability and is usually too low for an unattended production commitment. The
relevant threshold must come from the cost of failure and the review path
described in @sec-evaluating-agents. Changes to inference-time compute and
post-training can move the measured curve, but their effects must be identified
rather than assumed (cross-ref @sec-inference-time-scaling and
@sec-training-to-reason).
:::

## Trend estimates are conditional

Version 1.1 of the horizon suite shows how much of the measurement rests on
estimates. It expanded the benchmark from 170 to 228 tasks and included 31 tasks
estimated to take at least eight human hours. Only five of those 31 had measured
human baselines; the rest used estimates. In the January 2026 release, Claude
Opus 4.5 had a 50 percent horizon of 320 minutes, with an interval from 170 to
729 minutes [@metr2026timehorizon]. That is a wide interval around a roughly
five-hour point estimate.

The reported doubling time also changed with the regression window. The hybrid
Time Horizon 1.1 series gave 196.5 days over the full history, 130.8 days when
fit from 2023, and 88.6 days when fit from 2024. The three values come from
different fit windows, so they do not show one doubling time falling from seven
months to three within a few weeks. Task composition, baseline estimation, model
selection, and the short recent window all affect the trend.

By February and March 2026, METR reported a shared internal model with a 50
percent point from 16 to 20 hours and an 80 percent point from three to four
hours. The same report warned that the suite cannot reliably measure horizons
above 16 hours because only five tasks lie beyond that duration. The shared
internal model was not a named public checkpoint, and its runs used 16 to 64
million tokens, above earlier historical budgets [@metr2026riskreport]. The
result indicates that frontier systems were reaching the upper limit of what the
suite can measure. Because the model is not public and the token budgets are
larger, the result cannot be read as a continuation of the January public-model
series.

## Economic tasks measure deliverable preference

GDPval replaces exam questions with professional deliverables. Its full set has
1,320 tasks from 44 occupations in nine sectors of the US economy. Task writers
averaged 14 years of experience. The published launch evaluation used a
220-task open gold subset and asked occupation-matched experts to compare an
unlabeled model deliverable with the task writer's deliverable [@openai2025gdpval].

At launch, Claude Opus 4.1 received a better-or-equal judgment in 47.6 percent
of graded comparisons. The figure counts wins plus ties rather than wins alone,
and it is not a share of jobs automated. OpenAI's 23 April 2026 release later
reported GPT-5.5 at 84.9 percent wins plus ties on original GDPval, using xhigh
reasoning in a research environment [@openai2026gpt55]. The later release did
not disclose enough detail to assume that every sampling and judging choice
remained identical.

The tasks are one-shot, well-specified deliverables. They omit much of a job:
deciding what to do, gathering tacit context, negotiating requirements,
iterating with a customer, and bearing responsibility for the outcome. Claims
of roughly one-hundred-fold lower time or cost refer to pure model inference and
API accounting. They exclude human oversight, integration, iteration, and
rework. The 84.9 percent figure is therefore a benchmark preference rate, not an
occupation-automation rate.

RE-Bench measures a different object. It contains seven self-contained
machine-learning research-engineering environments. Its human comparison
comprised 61 distinct human experts making 71 eight-hour attempts. At a two-hour
total computer-time budget per environment, the best agent configuration
achieved about four times the average human normalized score. Humans narrowly
led at eight hours and reached about twice the best agent score at 32 hours
[@wijk2025rebench]. These are best-of-k results, the best score among $k$
attempts under a particular allocation of the budget, not necessarily one
continuous attempt. A normalized score on seven engineered environments is
informative about short-budget search, but it is not end-to-end research
automation.

```{dot}

//| fig-cap: "A benchmark deliverable is several links away from workplace value. Each link needs separate evidence; a high comparison score cannot establish the whole chain."

  nodesep=0.2; ranksep=0.22;
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9, color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280", fillcolor="#f1ece1", penwidth=1.1];
```

## Productivity needs its own measurement

A randomized study provides a concrete case of the gap between benchmark
capability and workplace productivity. From February to June 2025, 16 developers
with substantial open-source experience completed 246 tasks in repositories they
knew well. With access mainly to Cursor Pro and Claude 3.5 or 3.7 Sonnet, tasks
took 19 percent longer. Before the study, developers predicted they would be 24
percent faster; afterward, they believed they had been 20 percent faster
[@metr2025rct]. The result is limited to that sample, those tools, and those
tasks. It is still strong evidence that perceived speed and measured speed can
diverge.

A February 2026 follow-up produced raw estimates of an 18 percent speedup for
returning developers and a four percent speedup for new developers. METR called
both signals unreliable: returning participants and tasks were affected by
selection, compensation changed, and concurrent agent use made timing a poor
proxy [@becker2026upliftupdate]. The update does not overturn the randomized
result; it reports that the original protocol no longer measured newer workflows
well. Benchmark capability, task time, self-reported value, and causal
productivity are four different quantities. No stable conversion among them is
known.

## Benchmarks age in different ways

An instrument can lose value through ceiling effects, contamination (test items
or close duplicates entering training data), protocol drift, or exploitability.
These are different failures. A saturated benchmark may still detect regressions
in weaker systems; it has little headroom at the frontier. The 2026 paper on
Humanity's Last Exam (HLE) noted that frontier systems had passed more than 90
percent on MMLU, an older closed-answer academic benchmark, motivating a harder
set of 2,500 expert questions over more than 100 subjects [@hle2026].

HLE scores also depend on the protocol label. On August 7, 2026, the highest
score on the official Scale no-tools leaderboard was 46.44 percent. Separately
reported tool-enabled results exceeded 50 percent. No-tools and tool-enabled
scores cannot be placed on one curve, because retrieval and code execution
change the system under test [@scale2026hleleaderboard].

ARC-AGI-2 scores also rose quickly. Its May 2025 technical report placed leading
model baselines at less than 5 percent [@chollet2025arcagi2]. DeepMind reported
an ARC Prize-verified score of 84.6 percent in February 2026
[@deepmind2026arcagi2]. The model result and the reported human average came
from different evaluation sets that were calibrated for similar difficulty, not
from identical items. Compute, cost, and access conditions also differ. The 2026
competition still reserves a bonus threshold at 85 percent on a fully private
set. Under that protocol, the benchmark is not solved.

Construct validity concerns an earlier question, whether a score measures the
ability it claims to measure. A NeurIPS review had 29 experts examine 445
benchmark papers and ended with eight recommendations. It found recurring gaps
in construct definition, real-world task coverage, statistical testing, and
validity arguments; it did not show that every benchmark measures nothing
[@measuringwhatmatters2025]. A complementary General Scales study demonstrated
18 demand rubrics across 15 language models and 63 tasks, using instance
annotations to explain and predict difficulty. The method has been tested at
that scale and is not yet a general replacement for evaluation
[@hernandez2026generalscales].

Exploitability can be checked by attacking a benchmark. BenchJack's 2026
preprint audited ten agent benchmarks, catalogued 219 flaws, and synthesized
near-perfect exploits on nine of ten without solving the intended tasks
[@wang2026benchjack]. The audit was deliberately adversarial and used privileged
knowledge of the benchmarks, so it does not imply that ordinary model runs
always cheat. It shows that a score needs an adversarial audit before it can
support a broad capability claim.

The instruments saturate faster than they can be built in some fast-moving
domains. Saturation is also only one of the four failures named at the start of
this section, and some tests may never reach it. A replacement benchmark helps
only if its construct, protocol, and resistance to shortcuts improve with its
difficulty.

## Forecasts are scenarios

Trend extrapolation is useful when its assumptions stay visible. One exploratory
eight-parameter model projected more than 99 percent automation of AI research
and development tasks around 2032. Its author said the parameter values were
educated guesses, the model and write-up took roughly 15 hours, there was no
backtest, and he put little weight on the exact date [@metr2026timelines]. The
projection is a scenario, not a measurement, and it does not represent an
institutional consensus.

Picking a preferred trend fit cannot settle whether the gains are durable
progress or a compute-bought artifact. A continuation case needs evidence that
gains persist across frozen tasks, system budgets, and reliability thresholds. A
constraint case needs evidence that the growth rate falls once a named
resource becomes the limiting factor. Changes in reinforcement learning,
scaffolds, and test-time compute are candidate explanations; the horizon data
alone cannot establish any of them. @sec-scaling-laws covers the resource
mechanics.

::: {.callout-important}
## What's contested

- **What is moving?** The base model, scaffold, tools, budget, and task suite can
  all move a horizon. The field lacks one long, frozen protocol that isolates
  every contribution.
- **Which reliability matters?** Fifty percent is useful for tracking. A real
  deployment may require 80, 98, or more than 99 percent, depending on failure
  cost and review.
- **Do scores transfer to value?** Deliverable preference, research-environment
  score, elapsed task time, and workplace productivity are related but distinct.
- **Is fast benchmark improvement durable?** It can indicate improved capability,
  tool access, protocol drift, contamination, exploitation, or several at once.
- **How much weight should forecasts receive?** A transparent scenario exposes
  assumptions. It does not turn those assumptions into observations.
:::

## Keep a measurement ledger

A frontier claim is useful only when its contract travels with it. For every
result, record at least:

| Ledger field | What to record |
|---|---|
| Construct | The ability or outcome the result is meant to represent |
| Task sample | Inclusion rules, sampling frame, human-time baselines, and exclusions |
| System definition | Model checkpoint, agent scaffold, tools, prompts, and adaptation |
| Resource budget | Wall time, token and inference budget, retries, and parallelism |
| Repetitions | Runs per task, sampling policy, and dependence among attempts |
| Scorer | Success criteria, judge identity, tie handling, and adjudication |
| Integrity | Contamination checks, hidden sets, and adversarial audit results |
| Uncertainty | Intervals, task variation, judge variation, and sensitivity to fit choices |
| Snapshot | Measurement date, code and dataset version, and later protocol changes |
| Deployment link | Evidence connecting the benchmark construct to the intended workflow |
| Owner | The person responsible for rerunning, interpreting, and retiring the measure |

The ledger makes comparisons auditable without making any one benchmark
definitive. It also tells an organization when a result has expired because the
system, tasks, or deployment changed.

The frontier is therefore a set of moving, conditional limits. Horizon
measurements can show progress that saturated benchmarks miss, economic tasks
bring evaluation closer to work, and controlled studies test whether the value
survives deployment; none of the three substitutes for the others.
@sec-verification-frontier takes the next step: when a model can produce work
that an ordinary reviewer cannot cheaply verify, capability measurement gives
way to acceptance and control.
